title: John of God (8 March)
hookLine: a former soldier and bookseller who began caring for the sick, and whose followers became a hospital order

lines: LOCKED IN THE WARD FOR THE MAD.
cards: A street in Granada, in Spain. A man who sells holy books and pictures from a little shop stands in a crowd listening to the preacher John of Avila. Something in the sermon breaks him open.
He runs through the streets crying out for mercy, tearing up his own books, giving away everything in the shop.
The neighbors decide he has lost his mind, and he's taken to the city hospital and locked in the ward for the mad. That ward is where his story really begins. The Church calls him John of God.

teach.b: Before Granada, tradition says, John had been a shepherd, a soldier and a drifter, and none of it had gone well.

teach.h: BEATEN ON THE WARD FOR THE MAD.
teach.b: Inside, he saw what was done to people judged insane: on that ward, tradition says, they were beaten to drive the madness out, and so was John.
He made a decision there: if he ever got out, he would care for the sick the way he wished someone had cared for him and the men beside him.
John of Avila came to visit and calmed him, and once released, John did exactly that.

teach.h: A RENTED HOUSE AND A BASKET AT NIGHT.
teach.b: He rented a house, filled it with the sick and the homeless, and went out at night with a basket, begging for them.
Tradition says his cry in the streets was, roughly, do good, brothers, to yourselves: helping the poor was a gift to the giver. He washed patients, carried them on his back, and sorted them by need.
The bishop, tradition says, gave him the name John of God.
After his death his helpers carried on and became the Hospitaller Brothers of Saint John of God, a religious order devoted to the sick.
In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus describes the judgment, and kindness done to him in the least of people: "sick, and you visited me: I was in prison, and you came to me." John had been both.
A man once treated as mad became a patron of hospitals and the sick.

how: Catholics keep 8 March as the memorial of Saint John of God, patron of hospitals, nurses and the sick, and the Hospitaller Order he inspired runs hospitals and care homes that mark the day with Mass and celebrations for patients and staff.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is ill, or worn out caring for someone who is, and ask what would actually go in John's night basket for them: not flowers, but soup, a lift to an appointment, an hour so the carer can sleep.
If you pray, pray for them and those who care for them; if you don't, keep them in mind as you breathe.
